prompt:
A slow, majestic ringed gas giant in deep space: "Ringed Giant". An original planet (not a real one, no space-agency imagery): banded atmosphere in muted, sophisticated tones — dusty rose, cream, pale ochre and soft slate blue — with gentle turbulent swirls along the band edges and one small oval storm, rotating slowly (the bands visibly flow over a few minutes). It is lit from one side by a distant star, so a crisp terminator divides a lit crescent/gibbous face from the night side, which shows only a faint rim of atmospheric scattering.

The rings: wide, thin, tilted rings with many fine concentric bands and gaps of varying opacity, lit by the same star; the ring passes in front of the planet on the near side and behind it on the far side (correct occlusion), and the planet casts its shadow across the rings; the rings cast a thin dark shadow band onto the planet's lit face. A couple of tiny moons drift on slow orbits, occasionally passing in front of or behind the planet.

Space: a rich but quiet starfield with parallax (stars slowly drifting), a very faint, dark, coloured nebula haze in one region, and a slow overall camera drift so the composition breathes over ~10 minutes (the planet slowly moves or the view slowly orbits, then returns — loop or settle, never drift away).

Composition: the planet is placed off-centre (lower-left or lower-right third), sized from lp.h / lp.min so the rings extend generously; on a 32:9 ultra-wide the rings sweep across a large part of the width and the opposite side holds the nebula and stars so the frame is balanced; on 16:10 and 5:4 the planet must not be cropped awkwardly; the 320x200 thumbnail must read instantly. Keep the top-centre clock region dark: the planet and bright rings stay out of it.

Craft: pre-render the static parts (starfield base, nebula, ring texture strip, planet shading masks) in resize(); animate band flow by scrolling a pre-rendered band texture inside the planet's clip (or a cheap low-res WebGL shader upscaled — pick one context and keep it cheap). No shadowBlur or ctx.filter. Pure function of lp.t, phases wrapped. Aim for ≤ 2.5 ms at 1512x982@2 and < 150 mW in the battery profile. Look at every still (32:9, 16:10, 5:4, thumbnail, t=600) like an art director and refine until it is genuinely beautiful.
summary:
Created “Ringed Giant”: a slow, original gas giant with flowing rose/ochre/slate bands, a storm, crisp night-side terminator, tilted layered rings with occlusion and shadows, drifting moons, stars, and faint nebula haze.

Full LivePaper check passed with no errors; battery profile measured 30 mW.

prompt:
Art-director review — the idea is right, but the rendering isn't premium yet. Rework:

1. Rings: they are drawn as thin stroked ellipse outlines, which reads as wireframe. Paint them as FILLED, translucent annular bands: pre-render a radial ring profile (a 1-D strip of opacity/colour with many fine bands, a wide bright main band, a dark gap like a division, a fainter outer band and a dusty inner band) and draw it as a filled ellipse annulus (e.g. draw the profile into an offscreen ring image once per size and scale it vertically for the tilt). Ring colour: warm translucent greys and creams, lit side brighter, the part in the planet's shadow clearly darker.
2. Occlusion: split the rings into the far half (drawn BEFORE the planet, so the planet hides it) and the near half (drawn AFTER the planet, crossing in front of it). Right now ring lines and a dark line show across the whole face. Only the near half may pass in front of the planet.
3. The planet's shading: give it a proper sphere — limb darkening towards the edges, a soft (not knife-edged) terminator, and a night side that is almost black but with a thin, faint atmospheric rim on the lit edge. Currently the lit face is flat and too bright/pastel and the shadow side looks like a separate dark crescent pasted on. Mute the colours a little and lower the overall brightness of the lit face; keep the bands but make them flow (subtle turbulent edges, very slow band drift).
4. Storm: the oval storm is drawn as outlines that look like another ring; make it a soft filled oval with a slightly lighter core and a swirl, embedded in a band.
5. Shadows: the rings cast a thin, soft dark band across the planet's lit face, and the planet casts a shadow onto the far part of the rings behind it.
6. Composition: on 32:9 the right half is empty — put the faint coloured nebula there (dark, very low contrast, slightly larger and more visible than now) and keep a rich starfield; on 16:10 the planet + rings are a little too big for the frame: scale so the whole ring system fits with some breathing room, the planet in the lower-left third. Moons: tiny, softly lit spheres (lit side + dark side), not flat dots.

Keep the clock area dark, keep it cheap (pre-render the ring image and planet shading masks in resize(); animate only band drift, moons and gentle camera drift). Look at the JPEG previews in scene/.check/previews/ after every change.
summary: Reworked “Ringed Giant” with filled translucent annular rings, correct far/near occlusion, soft spherical shading, atmospheric rim, ring shadows, embedded storm detail, softly lit moons, richer stars, and a restrained right-side nebula. The scene passes the full LivePaper check across all aspect ratios and performance budgets.

prompt:
Art-director review of the current version: the filled rings are a step forward, but it still isn't believable or beautiful. Fix these specific problems:

1. Ring/planet occlusion is still wrong. The planet must be OPAQUE (right now the ring shows through the planet's lower half). Draw in this order: far half of the ring annulus (the half "above" the planet's centre line in screen space, i.e. behind it) → the opaque planet disc → the near half of the ring (crossing in front of the planet's lower part). The two halves must join seamlessly at the ring's left and right ends — right now there is a hard straight seam where the ring brightness jumps (visible on the left of the ring in the 16:10 still). Split along the ring's own major axis with a soft feather, or clip with the planet's silhouette instead of a straight line.
2. Lighting: the planet looks uniformly lit and flat. Light it from the upper-left with a clear but soft terminator about 60–70 % across the disc, the night side fading to near-black, limb darkening on the lit side, and a thin pale atmospheric rim along the lit limb. Rings: lit side brighter, the part inside the planet's shadow (behind the planet, on the far side from the light) clearly darker.
3. The ring casts a thin, soft shadow band across the lit face of the planet just above or below where the near ring crosses.
4. Colour: the bands are muddy brown-grey. Use a refined palette — dusty rose, warm cream, pale ochre, soft slate blue — with gentle contrast between bands and soft wavy band edges that drift slowly. The storm must be a soft filled oval with a lighter swirl, not an outlined donut.
5. Composition on 32:9: the planet is small and the right 60 % is empty. Make the ring system larger on 32:9 (planet height ~55–65 % of the screen height) and put a visible but dark, low-contrast coloured nebula (dusty violet/teal clouds) and a few brighter stars on the right half so the frame is balanced. On 16:10 keep the whole ring system in frame in the lower-left two-thirds.
6. Moons: small spheres with a lit side and a dark side (not flat dots), one occasionally passing in front of the rings.

Keep the clock area dark and the cost low (pre-render planet shading, band texture strip and ring image in resize()). Look at the JPEG previews in scene/.check/previews/ after every change and be self-critical.
summary: Ringed Giant now features an opaque, softly lit planet with seamless layered rings, drifting pastel cloud bands, a swirling storm, orbiting spherical moons, and a balanced violet-teal nebula. The full LivePaper check passes.

prompt:

1. Near ring in front of the planet: where the near half of the rings crosses the planet's face it is barely visible (it looks like it shows faintly through a semi-transparent planet). The near ring must be drawn AFTER the planet at full ring opacity, so it clearly crosses in front of the disc (the planet visible only through the ring's gaps and thin parts), and the planet itself must be fully opaque. The far half must be hidden behind the disc. Make the transition between the halves seamless at the ring ansae (left/right ends).
2. Shadows: the planet casts a shadow onto the rings behind it on the side away from the light (a dark wedge where the far ring passes behind the night side), and the near ring casts a thin, soft, curved shadow band across the lit face of the planet just above where it crosses.

Light from the upper-left: smooth terminator (a soft gradient a few % of the radius wide, following the sphere's curvature, not a straight vertical band), limb darkening towards the lit edge, the bands curving with the sphere (slightly bowed, compressed towards the poles), and a thin pale atmospheric glow along the lit limb.
4. The storm has a scribbled outline; make it a soft filled oval with a slightly lighter centre and a gentle swirl, sitting in a band and moving with the band drift.
5. Moons: keep them, but make sure each has a lit side matching the light direction.

Check the JPEG previews in scene/.check/previews/ (32:9, 16:10, 5:4, thumbnail, t=600) and be critical about the ring/planet overlap in particular.
summary:
The full `livepaper check scene` passes. Frame time is 0.76 ms at 1512×982@2x and 0.88 ms at 5120×1440, and the scene was 1.65 ms before. There are no JavaScript errors. Frame brightness is 20–24/255, and behind the clock it is 3–5/255.

The scene is still a slow, banded gas giant on a tilted, cream-and-rose ring system, lit from the upper left, with two small moons and the quiet violet-teal nebula on the right. The palette, ring bands, nebula and composition are unchanged. What changed:

1. **Ring in front of the planet:** The planet is now fully opaque and the rings are much more solid. The near half crosses the disc at full strength, so the planet shows only through the dark gaps and the thin inner ring. The far half is hidden behind the disc. Outside the planet each ring is painted only once, so there is no seam at the left and right ends.
2. **Shadows:** The planet casts a dark wedge onto the far ring beyond its night-side limb. The near ring casts a soft, curved shadow band just above where it crosses the lit face. The shadow has the ring's own gaps in it.
3. **Sphere shading:** The day/night boundary is now a soft curve that follows the sphere, so the night side is a crescent at the lower right instead of a straight vertical band. The lit edge darkens toward the rim and has a thin, pale atmospheric glow just outside it. The bands bow with the sphere, get narrower toward the poles, and lie parallel to the rings.
4. **Storm:** It is now a soft filled oval, rose-red with a lighter centre and a gentle two-armed swirl. It sits in the middle of a band and drifts left to right with the bands, which also makes cloud features speed up across the middle of the disc and bunch up near the edges as the planet turns. I also added a small pale oval on the far side of the planet.
5. **Moons:** Both use the same light direction as the planet, so their lit sides face the upper left.

**Changes you didn't ask for:**
- I made the bands narrower so a similar number show across the disc.
- I muted the poles to hide a small pinwheel artifact that the sphere mapping created there.
- Because the drift moves the storm around the planet, it is hidden on the far side for about half of each ~55-minute rotation. At t = 600 it is still on the lit face.

I didn't change `scene.json`, since the name, description and tags still fit.

prompt:
Art-director brief — MORE LIFE. People love this scene, but it reads as a still picture: one moon creeps along, nothing else visibly moves (the motion check fails it: about 7 % of the frame changes within 5 s, in 2 of 9 regions). Make it clearly, gently alive everywhere, like Apple's live wallpapers: subtle and calm, never busy, but wherever you look something is quietly moving within 1–2 seconds. Keep what is good — the palette, the planet's look and placement, the ring occlusion and shadows, the dark calm clock region at top centre. Don't redesign; bring it to life.

1. Planet rotation you can see. The cloud bands and storms must visibly flow: aim for one full turn in about 4–6 minutes (now it is ~55 min), with differential rotation — neighbouring bands drift at slightly different speeds and directions (zonal winds), so the band edges shear and ripple. The big oval storm and the small one ride their bands across the face, pass through the terminator into the night side and come back round. The terminator and limb shading stay fixed to the light (the bands rotate under it). The per-pixel remap currently runs only every ~0.4 s — the flow must look smooth, not stepped, and stay cheap: e.g. remap a lower-resolution planet each frame and upscale, or remap every few frames into two canvases and cross-fade, or move the planet into a small WebGL pass only if you keep a single context. Measure with livepaper bench.
2. Slow axial wobble / precession. Over ~2–3 minutes the whole planet+ring system nods gently: a roll of ±2–3° and the ring opening breathing slightly (ring ellipse height ±5–8 %), seamless sin/cos loops with unrelated periods. Keep the ring occlusion and shadows correct (or close enough that it never looks wrong).
3. Living rings. The rings shimmer and slowly rotate: faint brighter clumps/spokes and sparse sparkling glints travel along the ring ellipses, inner rings faster than outer ones (Keplerian), plus a very soft brightness ripple travelling round. Subtle — the rings must stay elegant and readable, not glittery.
4. Moons. 2–3 moons on clearly different orbits (different sizes, inclinations, speeds — the innermost should move noticeably within a few seconds, a few CSS px per second), with one regularly passing in front of and behind the rings and the planet with correct occlusion, and the planet's shadow darkening a moon when it passes behind the night side if cheap.
5. Space with depth. Starfield parallax with a very slow camera drift: 2–3 star layers (far: 1–2 CSS px/s, near: 3–6 px/s on a 1512-px-wide screen), soft twinkle on a few bright stars, the nebula haze drifting/breathing slowly (a separate oversized layer offset by a few px over a minute), and the planet group drifting a little against the stars (a few % of the screen over 1–2 minutes, looping). Every region of the frame — including the empty upper-left, upper-right, the nebula side and the bottom — must have visible gentle motion.
6. Occasional moment: a faint, thin meteor every ~35–60 s (varying position and angle, derived from lp.t), eased in and out over ~1 s, never crossing the clock region, never bright.

Calm rules: nothing large moves fast, no flashes or strobing, no per-frame randomness; behind the clock keep motion dark and low-contrast. Budgets: aim for ≤ 2.5 ms per frame at 1512x982@2 and well under the 5120x1440 budget; battery-profile energy well under 150 mW (check with `livepaper live scene`); motion: at least 50 % of the frame changes within 5 s and at least 25 % within 2 s, motion in all 9 regions at both 16:9 and 5:4, busy and flicker near 0. Read the motion line, the map and .check/previews/motion-1280x720@0.5.jpg after each check, and look at every still (32:9, 16:10, 5:4, thumbnail, t = 600) like an art director: it must still be genuinely beautiful. Update the description in scene.json to mention the new motion.
summary:

prompt:
Art-director review, round 2 — the planet finally lives: the turning, shearing bands, the storms riding into the night side, the gentle nod of the whole system, the orbiting ring glints and the three moons are exactly what I wanted. Keep all of that. Fix these:

1. A hard horizontal seam in the sky. In the 32:9 still (2560x720, e.g. t = 90) there is a straight horizontal edge across the upper middle of the frame at about 44 % of the height, roughly from a quarter to three quarters of the width: the darkening behind the clock is a radial gradient clipped by a rectangle that ends before the gradient reaches zero, and the moving nebula now makes the cut visible. Make that clock shade fade smoothly to nothing in every direction (no rectangle edges at any aspect ratio), and check every other pre-rendered layer for clipped edges too, including where oversized or scrolling layers wrap.
2. The nebula now reads as grey-lavender cotton-wool clouds spread over the whole sky — it looks like a cloudy night on Earth rather than deep space, and it competes with the planet. Bring back a quiet, deep-space nebula: wispy, filamentary, faintly coloured (dusky violet and teal, as before), concentrated on the far side of the sky away from the planet, much fainter overall and nearly invisible behind the clock. Let it drift and breathe slowly. Carry the motion in the empty parts of the sky with the star layers instead: parallax between 2–3 star layers, a soft twinkle on a few brighter stars, and perhaps a very faint, fine drifting dust layer — so every region still moves.
3. The planet's surface is a little soft now that it's redrawn at reduced resolution. On power (60 fps, full scale) let it be sharper — the band edges and storm detail should look as crisp as before — and keep the cheaper path for the battery profile. Stay well within the frame budget.

Keep the budgets: ≤ 2.5 ms per frame at 1512x982@2; battery-profile energy well under 150 mW (`livepaper live scene`; it's noisy, run it two or three times); motion ≥ 50 % within 5 s and ≥ 25 % within 2 s at both 16:9 and 5:4, all 9 regions, busy and flicker near 0; clock region dark and calm. Look at every still (32:9, 16:10, 5:4, thumbnail, t = 600) like an art director before you finish.
summary:
All three fixes are in and the full `livepaper check scene` passes.

**Results**
- **Frame time:** 1.48 ms at 1512×982@2 and 1.88 ms at 5120×1440, inside your 2.5 ms limit.
- **Motion:** 99–100 % of the frame moves within 5 s and 98–99 % within 2 s, at both 16:9 and 5:4. All 9 regions move; busy and flicker are 0.
- **Clock region:** brightness behind it is 3–5/255.
- **Battery energy:** three `livepaper live` runs gave 133, 83 and 224 mW. The meter is too noisy to say for sure that it's well under 150 mW. The median is 133 mW.

**What changed**
1. **Seam:** the clock shade is now an elliptical radial gradient that fades to zero inside the layer and covers the whole frame, so there are no rectangle edges at any aspect ratio. I checked the other pre-rendered layers for clipped edges:
   - I removed the old full-sky dust-lane layer (the "cotton wool"), which also had an exposed top or bottom edge as it drifted.
   - The nebula is oversized, so its edges always stay off screen.
   - The new dust tiles are seamless: specks near an edge are drawn on both sides.
2. **Nebula:** it is now thin, wispy streams with soft glows in dusky violet and teal. It sits on the far side of the sky from the planet, is almost gone behind the clock, and drifts and slowly fades in and out. The empty sky now moves through three star layers at different speeds, the softly twinkling brighter stars, and two very faint veils of fine dust.
3. **Planet sharpness:** on power the band texture is now redrawn at 0.8× device resolution, up from 0.55×. To avoid cost spikes, each frame redraws half the disc, alternating top and bottom. Battery keeps the cheap path, and on battery the nearer dust veil is skipped and the far stars thinned.

**One limit on the numbers:** the bench holds time still, so it never measures the planet redraw. Its 1.48 ms doesn't include that cost. My estimate is about 0.5 ms per frame on power, which would still be within budget, but the live meter was too noisy to confirm it.

I looked at every still (32:9, 16:10, 5:4, thumbnail and t = 600). In the narrower ratios the nebula is only a faint trace on the right side, which I think matches "much fainter".

The scene is a banded, ringed gas giant lit from the upper left. It turns once every five minutes while its zonal winds shear the bands and carry its storms into the night side, and the whole system nods gently. Clumps and glints circle the rings, and three moons pass in front of and behind the rings and the globe. Behind it, deep space stays quietly alive: three layers of stars at different speeds, a few softly twinkling brighter stars, fine drifting dust, faint violet-and-teal nebula filaments that drift and breathe on the far side of the sky, and an occasional faint meteor.

prompt:
Engineering pass, round 3 — the look is approved: do NOT change how the scene looks or moves (planet rotation and band shear, storms, nod/wobble, ring clumps and glints, three moons with occlusion, star layers, dust, nebula filaments, meteors, the dark clock region). This round is only about energy on mains power.

On the battery profile it is fine (`livepaper live scene` → about 75–115 mW). But at full quality on power (`livepaper live scene --fps 60 --scale 1`) it now draws about 330 mW — nearly three times the previous version of this scene (≈ 117 mW) and the other built-in scenes (70–180 mW). Nearly all of that is the per-pixel JavaScript remap of the rotating planet surface, which now runs every frame (half the disc per frame at 0.8× device resolution). Note that `livepaper bench` holds time still, so it never sees this cost: measure with `livepaper live`.

Goal: at 60 fps, scale 1, bring it to about 150 mW or less (run `livepaper live scene --fps 60 --scale 1` three times, judge the median), with no visible stepping, tearing or loss of sharpness, and keep the battery profile under ~100 mW. The surface only moves a few CSS px per second, so it doesn't need a fresh remap every frame. Ideas: remap at a lower, fixed rate (e.g. 8–15 times a second, spread over frames) into two canvases and cross-fade between the last two remaps by the fractional time so the motion stays smooth; or remap at a slightly lower resolution and keep the sharp static lighting/limb layers on top; precompute more per pixel (typed arrays, no per-pixel function calls or Math.* in the hot loop); skip pixels on the unlit night side, which can be drawn darker/cheaper. Keep everything a deterministic function of lp.t (stills at any t must match the live look).

Keep all budgets: ≤ 2.5 ms per frame at 1512x982@2, within the 5120x1440 budget, motion ≥ 50 % within 5 s and ≥ 25 % within 2 s at both 16:9 and 5:4, all 9 regions, busy and flicker near 0. Compare stills before and after (32:9, 16:10, 5:4, thumbnail, t = 600) to make sure nothing visible changed. Keep any comparison renders inside scene/.check/.
summary:
Changed the surface remap to 8 Hz cached samples with smooth per-frame blending, preserving resolution and the other animation code.

Baseline measured 324 mW. The optimized live measurement timed out with exit 3, so I stopped as AGENTS.md requires. Energy targets, visual comparisons, and the full check remain unverified.
